concepts.title: Differences in Spatial Extent

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: CNNs use kernels with non-unitary spatial extent to process adjacent regions, whereas transformers use 1x1 filters to maintain permutation invariance.
concepts.content: CNNs can have kernels with non-unitary spatial extent, whereas the query-key-value projections and token-wise MLPs in transformers only use 1x1 filters. A 1x1 filter refers to any filter whose kernel size is 1 in all its dimensions, regardless of the signal's dimensionality. This architectural choice is necessary for transformers to maintain permutation invariance; using a larger kernel would make the filter output depend on the relative positioning of tokens. While CNNs use $K \times K$ filters to process adjacent image regions together, transformers have no architectural way of knowing about spatial structure. For vision problems where spatial structure is crucial, transformers are instead provided with positional knowledge through the inputs to the network.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains the fundamental architectural trade-off between CNNs and transformers. CNNs are designed to exploit local spatial structure through multi-pixel kernels, while transformers prioritize permutation invariance and global interactions, requiring external positional information to understand spatial relationships.

concepts.title: Attention vs. Convolution Locality

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Unlike convolutional layers that process independent local chunks, attention layers perform global operations where all input tokens can interact.
concepts.content: Attention layers are not convolutional. They do not factor the processing into independent chunks but instead perform a global operation, in which all input tokens can interact. The resulting linear combination of tokens is not a mixing operation found in CNNs and addresses the limitation of CNNs being myopic, where each filter only sees information within its specific receptive field.
concepts.motivation_md: CNNs are limited by their local receptive fields, meaning they cannot easily capture long-range dependencies. Attention layers solve this by allowing every token to communicate with every other token regardless of distance.

concepts.title: Masked Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Masked attention restricts token interactions by fixing specific weights in the attention matrix to zero, often to enforce causality in sequential prediction.
concepts.content: Masked attention restricts which tokens can attend to which by fixing some of the weights to be zero. This is useful for learning features via masked autoencoding, cross-attention between different data modalities, and sequential prediction. For example, in predicting the $(n+1)$-th token given the previous $n$ tokens, we can use a single matrix multiply to make multiple predictions at once. (see figure: Masked prediction of time index 4 from time indices 1-3.) During training, we provide examples where sub-sequences predict the next token: $$\begin{aligned} \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_n\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n+1}\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-1}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_n\\ \{\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_{n-2}\} &\rightarrow \mathbf{t}_{n-1} \end{aligned}$$ This is achieved in a single forward pass using a masked matrix. (see figure: Masked attention to make multiple causal predictions at once. Black cells are masked; they are filled with zeros.) This approach, called causal attention when applied to an attention matrix, speeds up training by supervising all sub-sequence problems simultaneously. In multi-layer transformers, this masking ensures that output tokens at any layer only depend on previous tokens from the input. (see figure: Multilayer masked attention achieves causal prediction with a deep net.)
concepts.motivation_md: Masking allows transformers to handle sequential data without 'cheating' by looking at future information. It also enables highly efficient parallel training for autoregressive tasks.

concepts.title: Causal Attention

concepts.one_liner: Causal attention is a masking strategy where each token only attends to previous tokens in a sequence to enable efficient sequential prediction.
concepts.content: Causal attention is a masking strategy where each token can only attend to previous tokens in the sequence. An attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is called causal because each output index $i$ only depends on input indices $j$ such that $j < i$. This approach can dramatically speed up training because all sub-sequence prediction problems—such as predicting $\mathbf{t}_{n-1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-2}$, predicting $\mathbf{t}_{n}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n-1}$, and predicting $\mathbf{t}_{n+1}$ given $\mathbf{T}_{1:n}$—are supervised at the same time during a single forward pass.
concepts.motivation_md: In tasks like language modeling, a model must not see the 'future' tokens it is trying to predict. Causal attention enforces this constraint while allowing the entire sequence to be processed in parallel during training.

concepts.title: Positional Encoding

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Positional encoding concatenates a code representing a token's position within a signal to restore spatial knowledge lost due to permutation equivariance.
concepts.content: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, meaning tokens do not inherently encode their position within a signal. Positional encoding addresses this by concatenating a code representing the position within the signal onto each token. For images, these codes represent x- and y-coordinates, often using a periodic representation where coordinates are encoded as vectors of values from sinusoidal waves: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{p}_x &= [\sin(x), \sin(x/B), \sin(x/B^2), \ldots, \sin(x/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p}_y &= [\sin(y), \sin(y/B), \sin(y/B^2), \ldots, \sin(y/B^P)]^\mathsf{T}\\ \mathbf{p} &= \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p}_x\\ \mathbf{p}_y \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ (see figure: Positional codes.) Alternatively, positional codes can be learned by the model. While common in transformers, these encodings can also be used in CNNs to condition filters on position or in radiance fields.
concepts.motivation_md: Because transformers treat inputs as unordered sets, they are 'blind' to the structure of sequences or images. Positional encodings provide the necessary context for the model to understand where each piece of information is located.
concepts.recap_md: [RECAP_MD]

key_passage.text: Positional encoding concatenates a code representing position within the signal onto each token. If the signal is an image, then the positional code should represent the x- and y-coordinates. However, it need not represent these coordinates as scalars; more commonly we use a periodic representation of position, where the coordinates are encoded as the vector of values a set of sinusoidal waves take on at each position.

motivation.text: Operations over tokens in a transformer are permutation equivariant, which means that we can shuffle the positions of the tokens and nothing substantial changes. A consequence is that tokens do not know encode their position within the representation of the signal. Sometimes, however, we may wish to retain positional knowledge. For example, knowing that a token is a representation of the top region of an image can help us identify that the token is likely to represent sky.

position.section_title: Comparing Fully Connected, Convolutional, and Self-Attention Layers

concepts.one_liner: Fully-connected, convolutional, and self-attention layers are all affine transformations that differ in how their weight matrices are structured and determined.
concepts.content: Fully-connected (`fc`), convolutional (`conv`), and self-attention (`attn`) layers are all types of affine transformations where the forward pass is written as $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$. In `conv` and `attn` layers, $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are determined as functions of the input $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$. For `conv` layers, this function creates a Toeplitz matrix repeating the convolutional kernels. For `attn` layers, the function determining $\mathbf{W}$ is more complex, and biases $\mathbf{b}$ are typically not used. While the matrix for an `fc` layer is full rank, `conv` and `attn` matrices exhibit different kinds of low-rank structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these layers as specific types of matrix operations helps unify deep learning theory, showing how different architectures impose different constraints (priors) on the weight matrix $\mathbf{W}$.
concepts.recap_md: [RECAP_MD]

key_passage.text: All these layers are alike in that their forward pass can be written as $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$ for some matrix $\mathbf{W}$ and some vector $\mathbf{b}$. In `conv` and `attn` layers, $\mathbf{W}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are determined as some function of the input $\mathbf{X}_{\texttt{in}}$.

motivation.text: Each of these layers can be represented as a matrix, and examining the structure in these matrices can be a useful way to understand their similarities and differences.

concepts.title: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a general class of architectures that process sets by forming a graph of operations over the input elements.
concepts.content: Transformers can be considered a special case of graph neural networks (GNNs). GNNs are a general class of architecture for processing sets by forming a graph of operations over the set. A transformer functions by taking an input set of tokens and, layer by layer, applying a network of transformations over that set until a final representation or prediction is produced.
concepts.motivation_md: GNNs provide a mathematical framework for data that doesn't fit into a rigid grid, like social networks or molecules. Transformers adapt this for sequences and images by treating tokens as nodes in a fully connected graph.
concepts.recap_md: [RECAP_MD]

key_passage.text: GNNs are a very general class of architecture for processing *sets* by forming a graph of operations over the set. A transformer is doing exactly that: it takes an input set of tokens and, layer by layer, applies a network of transformations over that set until after enough layers a final representation or prediction is read out.

motivation.text: We do not have a separate chapter on GNNs in this book since GNNs, other than transformers, are not yet popular in computer vision.

concepts.title: The Full Transformer Architecture

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities, often augmented with normalization layers and residual connections.
concepts.content:
A full transformer architecture is a stack of self-attention layers interleaved with tokenwise nonlinearities. These two steps are analogous to linear layers interleaved with neuronwise nonlinearities in an MLP.

(see figure: The basic transformer architecture versus an MLP.)

Beyond this basic template, there are many variations that can be added, resulting in different particular architectures within the transformer family. Some common additions are normalization layers and residual connections. In (see figure: The ViT transformer architecture~\cite{dosovitskiy2020vit}. This set of layers forms a computational block, shaded in gray, that can be repeated $L$ times for a depth $L$ ViT. To clarify where the...) we see the ViT architecture, showing where these additional pieces enter the picture.

This architecture uses layer normalization before each attention layer and before each token-wise MLP layer. The normalization is performed within each token, where the token code vector is treated akin to a layer; each dimension is standardized by the mean and variance over all dimensions of that vector. This operation is referred to as `token norm`. Residual connections are added around each group of layers.

The output of a transformer is a set of tokens $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$. To produce a different format, such as a single vector of logits for image classification or an image for image-to-image tasks, a task-specific output layer is typically defined. For example, to produce logit predictions, one could sum all the token code vectors in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}$ and then project the resulting $d$-dimensional vector into a $K$-dimensional vector using a single linear layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Transformers solve the problem of processing sequences or sets of data by interleaving global information sharing (attention) with independent local processing (tokenwise MLPs). This modular structure allows the model to scale effectively while maintaining the flexibility to handle various input and output formats through task-specific heads.

concepts.title: Permutation Equivariance

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Transformers are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence because their constituent layers—attention and tokenwise MLPs—are themselves permutation equivariant.
concepts.content:
An important property of transformers is that they are equivariant to permutations of the input token sequence. This follows from the fact that both tokenwise layers, $F_{\theta}$, and attention layers, $\texttt{attn}$, are permutation equivariant:

$$\begin{aligned}
    F_{\theta}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))\\
    \texttt{attn}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{attn}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

where $\texttt{permute}$ is a permutation of the order of tokens in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$ (i.e., permutes the rows of the matrix). This means that if you scramble the patches in the input image then apply attention, the output will be unchanged up to a permutation of the original output. Since the full transformer architecture is a composition of these two types of layers (plus residual connections and token normalization, which are also permutation equivariant), and because composing two permutation equivariant functions results in a permutation equivariant operation, we have:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{transformer}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{transformer}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

This property is visualized in (see figure: Transformers are permutation equivariant. For notational simplicity, we omit layer indices on the token variables here.).
concepts.motivation_md: Permutation equivariance ensures that the model treats the input as a set of entities rather than a fixed grid, allowing it to process information based on content and relationships rather than just absolute spatial position.

This means that if you scramble the patches in the input image then apply attention, the output will be unchanged up to a permutation of the original output. Since the full transformer architecture is a composition of these two types of layers (plus residual connections and token normalization, which are also permutation equivariant), and because composing two permutation equivariant functions results in a permutation equivariant operation, we have:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \texttt{transformer}(\texttt{permute}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}})) &= \texttt{permute}(\texttt{transformer}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}))
\end{aligned}$$

This property is visualized in (see figure: Transformers are permutation equivariant. For notational simplicity, we omit layer indices on the token variables here.).

concepts.title: Equivariance and Invariance in Layers

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Layers can be categorized by their symmetries, with attention being both translation and permutation equivariant, while convolutions are translation equivariant but not necessarily permutation equivariant.
concepts.content:
It is often useful to understand layers in terms of their invariances and equivariances. Convolutational layers are translation equivariant but not necessarily permutation equivariant, whereas attention layers are both translation equivariant and permutation equivariant. Since translation is a special kind of permutation, any permutation equivariant layer is also translation equivariant. Other layers can be catalogued similarly: global average pooling layers are permutation invariant, ReLU layers are permutation equivariant, and per-token MLP layers are also permutation equivariant (with respect to sets of tokens rather than sets of neurons).

A generally good strategy is to select layers that reflect the symmetries in your data or task. In object detection, translation equivariance makes sense because a bird is a bird no matter where it appears in an image. Permutation equivariance might also make sense for the same reason, but only to an extent: if you break up an image into small patches and scramble them, this could disrupt spatial layout that is important for recognition. Transformers address this by using positional codes to reinsert information about spatial layout.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the symmetries of different layers helps in designing architectures that naturally respect the properties of the data, such as the spatial consistency required for image recognition.

concepts.title: Tokenization as Convolution

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Tokenization in transformers can be implemented as a convolutional layer where the kernel size and stride are both equal to the patch size $K$.
concepts.content:
The first step in working with transformers is to tokenize the input. The most basic way to do this is to chop up the input image into non-overlapping patches of size $K \times K$, then convert these patches to vectors via a linear projection. This operation can be written as a convolution with kernel size and stride both equal to $K$:

$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbf{T}[n(N/K)+m,c_{\texttt{2}}] = \nonumber\\
&b[c_{\texttt{2}}] +  \sum_{c_{\texttt{1}}=1}^{C_{\texttt{in}}} \sum_{k_1,k_2=-K}^K w[c_{\texttt{1}},c_{\texttt{2}},k_1,k_2] x_{\texttt{in}}[c_{\texttt{1}},K n-k_1,K m-k_2] \quad \triangleleft \quad \text{(tokenization)}
\end{aligned}$$

where, for RGB images, $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}\in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N \times M}$, $C_{\texttt{in}}=3$, and $C_{\texttt{out}}=d$ (the token dimensionality). This assumes $N$ and $M$ are evenly divisible by $K$. In code, this is a `conv` operator:

```python
T = conv(x_in, channels_in=3, channels_out=d, kernel=K, stride=K) # tokenize
```
concepts.motivation_md: Representing tokenization as a convolution allows the initial processing of an image into discrete tokens to be performed efficiently using standard deep learning hardware and operations.

concepts.title: Query-Key-Value Projections as Convolutions

concepts.one_liner: The query, key, and value projections in attention layers are equivalent to multichannel convolutions with a kernel size of 1.
concepts.content: The query, key, and value projections in attention layers apply the same linear transformation to each token vector. Applying the same linear operation to each element in a sequence is exactly what convolution does. Specifically, the query operation $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{W}_q^\mathsf{T}$ can be written as convolving the set of $N$ $d$-channel tokens with a filter bank of $m$ filters, with kernel size 1, producing a new set of $N$ $m$-channel tokens. This equivalence is visualized in (see figure: The query, key, and value projections in transformers can be written either as a convolution or a matrix multiply.). Therefore, the query, key, and value projections are all multichannel convolutions with kernels of size 1.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing projections as $1 \times 1$ convolutions highlights the architectural similarity between transformers and CNNs, showing that transformers use standard local operations to prepare data for global attention.

concepts.title: Tokenwise MLP as CNN

concepts.one_liner: A tokenwise MLP layer in a transformer can be mathematically represented as a series of $1 \times 1$ convolutions interleaved with neuronwise nonlinearities, effectively forming a CNN.
concepts.content: A token-wise MLP applies the same MLP $F_{\theta}$ to each token in a sequence. This $F_{\theta}$ consists of linear layers and pointwise nonlinearities. The linear layers take the form $\mathbf{t}_{\texttt{out}} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{t}_{\texttt{in}}$. When applied to the entire sequence, this becomes $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}\mathbf{W}^{\mathsf{T}}$. This operation is identical to the query projection and can be written as a convolution with kernel size 1. Since the pointwise nonlinearities in the MLP function identically to the pointwise nonlinearities in CNNs, a token-wise MLP can be written as a series of convolutions interleaved with neuronwise-nonlinearities—that is, a CNN.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing tokenwise MLPs as CNNs helps unify the theory of different neural network architectures, demonstrating that transformers heavily utilize convolutional principles for local feature transformation.
concepts.recap_md: - Tokenwise MLPs are equivalent to CNNs using $1 \times 1$ kernels.

This is the full set of layers in the MLP, and therefore we have that a token-wise MLP can be written as a series of convolutions interleaved with neuronwise-nonlinearities, i.e. a CNN.

concepts.title: Token Matrix Notation

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: A sequence of tokens is represented by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$ where each row is a transposed token vector.
concepts.content:
A sequence of tokens is denoted by a matrix $\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$, in which each token in the sequence, $\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N$, is transposed to become a row of the matrix:

$$\mathbf{T} = 
  \begin{bmatrix}
    \mathbf{t}_1^\mathsf{T}\\
    \vdots \\
    \mathbf{t}_N^\mathsf{T}\\
\end{bmatrix}$$

Graphically, $\mathbf{T}$ is constructed from $\mathbf{t}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{t}_N$ as shown in (see figure: In this chapter, we will represent a set of tokens as a matrix whose rows are the token vectors.).

Transformers are invariant to permutations of the input sequence, so groups of tokens should be thought of as sets rather than ordered sequences. This notation implies that tokens are to transformers as neurons are to neural nets. While neural net layers operate over arrays of neurons (column vectors), transformers operate over arrays of tokens represented by the matrix $\mathbf{T}$. Although we primarily consider vector-valued tokens, tokens could theoretically be any structured group as long as basic operators like summation are defined.
concepts.motivation_md: To process groups of vectors efficiently using linear algebra, we need a standardized mathematical representation. Organizing tokens as rows in a matrix allows us to use matrix multiplication to perform operations on all tokens simultaneously.

concepts.title: Mixing Tokens

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Mixing tokens involves taking a linear combination of vector-valued tokens, analogous to how neural nets take weighted sums of scalar neurons.
concepts.content:
Once data is converted to tokens, we define operations for transforming them, starting with the linear combination of tokens. Unlike a fully connected layer in a standard neural net that sums scalar neurons, this operation takes a weighted sum of vector-valued tokens. (see figure: Linear combination of neurons versus tokens.)

The general form for these equations is:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}[i,:]&= \sum_{j=1}^N w_{ij} \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[j,:]\\
     \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}
\end{aligned}$$

Operations over tokens are defined similarly to operations over neurons, but with vector values. For example, a fully connected layer (fc layer) over tokens maps $N_1$ input tokens to $N_2$ output tokens using a weight matrix $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_2 \times N_1}$ and optional token biases $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_2 \times d}$:

$$\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= \mathbf{W}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}+ \mathbf{b}$$
concepts.motivation_md: To share information across different parts of an input (like different patches of an image), the network must be able to combine information from multiple tokens. Linear mixing provides a mathematically simple way to aggregate these features.

concepts.title: Modifying Tokens

concepts.one_liner: Tokenwise operators apply nonlinear transformations to each token individually and independently, allowing the model to represent complex, non-linear functions.
concepts.content:
Linear combinations only allow for linear mixing; to model nonlinear functions, we introduce tokenwise operators. These functions apply a nonlinear transformation $F_{\theta}: \mathbb{R}^N \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^N$ to each token individually and independently. A tokenwise nonlinearity layer is expressed as:

$$\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= 
        \begin{bmatrix}
        F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[0,:]) \\
        \vdots \\
        F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[N-1,:]) \\
        \end{bmatrix}$$

This generalizes pointwise nonlinearities in regular neural nets (like ReLU). A key difference is that while standard neuronwise nonlinearities like ReLU usually have no learnable parameters, the tokenwise function $F_{\theta}$ is often a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with its own learnable weights and biases, making these operations highly expressive.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers alone cannot solve complex problems because the composition of linear functions is still linear. Tokenwise nonlinearities allow the network to learn complex features within each token's vector space.

$$\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}= 
        \begin{bmatrix}
        F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[0,:]) \\
        \vdots \\
        F_{\theta}(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}[N-1,:]) \\
        \end{bmatrix}$$

This generalizes pointwise nonlinearities in regular neural nets (like ReLU). A key difference is that while standard neuronwise nonlinearities like ReLU usually have no learnable parameters, the tokenwise function $F_{\theta}$ is often a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with its own learnable weights and biases, making these operations highly expressive.

concepts.title: Multihead Self-Attention

concepts.one_liner: Multihead self-attention (MSA) runs multiple attention layers in parallel to measure token similarity in several different ways simultaneously.
concepts.content:
Multihead self-attention (MSA) addresses the limitation of single-headed attention, which only uses one set of projection matrices to define similarity. By running $k$ attention layers in parallel on the same input $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$, the model can measure similarity in multiple ways (e.g., by color, texture, or shape). 

The $k$ output sets of tokens $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^1, \ldots, \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^k$ are concatenated and projected back to the original dimensionality $d$ using a learnable matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$:

$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}^i &= \texttt{attn}^i(\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}) \\
    \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}} &= [\text{concatenation of heads}] \\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}} &= \bar{\mathbf{T}}_{\texttt{out}}\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}
\end{aligned}$$

In MSA, the value vectors do not need to match the output token dimensionality because the final projection $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{MSA}}$ handles the mapping. This allows the network to add more parallel self-attention layers to increase expressivity.
concepts.motivation_md: A single attention head can only focus on one type of relationship at a time. Multihead attention allows the model to simultaneously attend to different features, such as both the syntax and the semantics of a word, or both the color and the shape of an object.

concepts.one_liner: Transformers are architectures that use attention layers to model dependencies between independent chunks of data in parallel.
concepts.content: Transformers are a family of architectures that generalize and expand the ideas behind convolutional neural nets (CNNs). Like CNNs, transformers factorize the signal processing problem into stages that involve independent and identically processed chunks. However, they also include attention layers that mix information across the chunks so that the full pipeline can model dependencies between them. Although often presented as an alternative to recurrent neural nets (RNNs) for sequence modeling, transformer layers are parallel processing machines rather than sequential machines.

concepts.title: Attention Layer

concepts.one_liner: Attention layers use data-dependent weights to define linear combinations of tokens, allowing the network to dynamically focus on specific information.
concepts.content:
Attention layers define a special kind of linear combination of tokens. Rather than parameterizing the linear combination with a matrix of free parameters $\mathbf{W}$, attention layers use a data-dependent attention matrix $\mathbf{A}$. The values of $\mathbf{A}$ are a function of the data input to the network and typically contain non-negative values, representing how much attention is paid to each input token. (see figure: Fully-connected layers versus attention layers.)

Attention can be described as a kind of dynamic pooling, where a weighted average is used and the weights are dynamically decided based on the input data. The equation for an attention layer is:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{A} &= f(\ldots) \quad\quad \triangleleft \text{ attention}\\
    \mathbf{T}_{\texttt{out}}&= \mathbf{A}\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}
\end{aligned}$$

The function $f$ determines how much attention to apply to each token in $\mathbf{T}_{\texttt{in}}$. For example, to count animals in an image, $f$ might take a text query and produce weights $\mathbf{A}$ that are high for tokens representing animal heads and low for others. (see figure: How attention can be allocated across different regions (tokens) in an image. The token code vectors consist of multiple dimensions and each can encode a different attribute of the token. To the left...)

This mechanism allows the layer to dynamically change its behavior in response to different inputs. A common version of this function used in transformers is called query-key-value attention.
concepts.motivation_md: Fixed weights in standard layers cannot adapt to the specific content of an input. Attention allows a model to "look" at different parts of the input depending on the context or task.
concepts.recap_md:
- Attention layers use data-dependent weights ($\mathbf{A}$) rather than fixed learned parameters ($\mathbf{W}$).
- They allow the network to dynamically focus on specific tokens based on their relevance to a query.

position.section_title: A Limitation of CNNs: Independence between Far Apart Patches

concepts.one_liner: CNNs are limited by their local focus, making it difficult and computationally expensive to share information between distant regions of an image.
concepts.content:
CNNs are built around the idea of locality, assuming that different local regions of an image can be processed independently using filters with small kernels. However, global information often needs to be shared across all receptive fields. Convolutional layers are not well-suited to globalizing information because they must either increase kernel sizes or stack many layers to expand the receptive field. (see figure: Consider a 2-layer CNN with kernel size 3, tasked to compare $x_1$ and $x_7$. It can't do it: there are no neurons that are connected to both $x_1$ and $x_7$. Hatch marks indicate which neurons are...)

While fully connected layers can pass messages across large spatial distances, they require $N^2$ parameters for $N$-dimensional vectors, which can take an exorbitant amount of time and data to fit.

- Expanding receptive fields via stacking layers or increasing kernel size is inefficient for global information sharing.

concepts.title: The Idea of Attention

position.chapter_title: T now contains the output token representation computed by the transformer

concepts.one_liner: Attention is a strategy for efficiently processing global information by focusing on the most salient parts of a signal for a given task.
concepts.content: Attention is a strategy for processing global information efficiently by focusing on the parts of the signal that are most salient to the task at hand. This idea is motivated by human perception; when viewing a scene, our eyes attend to specific elements that stand out rather than taking in the whole scene at once. In neural networks, attention follows this same intuition: a set of neurons on one layer may attend to a set of neurons on a previous layer to decide their response. For example, if asked to report the color of a car, neurons should direct their attention to the previous-layer neurons representing that car.
concepts.motivation_md: Processing every part of a high-dimensional input with equal weight is computationally wasteful. Attention allows models to prioritize relevant information, similar to how biological vision systems operate.
concepts.recap_md:
- Attention mimics human perception by focusing on salient features rather than the entire input.
- It allows neurons to dynamically select which information from previous layers is relevant to the current task.
